nameStory: The treetop bush katydid gets its name from its preference for living high up in the canopy of trees and tall shrubs, unlike many of its ground-dwelling cricket cousins. It's also called the black-striped katydid because of the dark bands that decorate its green body. The scientific name honors Samuel Scudder, a 19th-century American entomologist who was passionate about studying grasshoppers and their relatives.
description: The treetop bush katydid is a slender, green insect that looks like a living leaf with legs. These delicate creatures are about 1-2 inches long and have incredibly long, thread-like antennae that can be twice the length of their body. Their wings are narrow and translucent with dark stripes, and their long hind legs are built for jumping rather than the powerful kicks of grasshoppers. Like all katydids, they're more closely related to crickets than grasshoppers, belonging to the group of insects known as Orthoptera.

idTips.label: Dark wing stripes
idTips.description: Look for distinctive black or dark brown stripes running along the pale green, papery wings - these bands are the katydid's signature feature and feel thin as tissue paper when gently touched

idTips.label: Thread-like antennae
idTips.description: The antennae are extremely long and hair-thin, often longer than the entire body, and constantly move in a gentle swaying motion as the insect explores its surroundings

idTips.label: Leaf-like body shape
idTips.description: The overall body is elongated and flattened, with a narrow profile that mimics a blade of grass or thin leaf - the texture feels smooth and slightly waxy

idTips.label: Delicate build
idTips.description: Much more slender and fragile-looking than robust grasshoppers, with thin legs and a lightweight feel if one lands on your hand

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Bright to pale green color that perfectly matches new growth on trees and shrubs, sometimes with yellowish tints on the legs and underside

habitat: Treetop bush katydids live in the upper branches and canopy of deciduous trees and tall shrubs throughout New England's forests and woodland edges. You'll find them in oak, maple, and birch trees, as well as in overgrown areas where shrubs like elderberry and sumac create dense thickets. They prefer areas with mixed vegetation rather than pure stands of single tree species.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet present, but eggs laid the previous fall begin developing in tree bark crevices and plant stems.
seasonality.summer: Young nymphs appear in early summer, looking like miniature wingless versions of adults as they climb through the foliage feeding on leaves.
seasonality.fall: Adults reach maturity and begin their distinctive nighttime chorus of chirping calls, with peak activity in late August through September before the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frost, leaving behind eggs that will survive the winter tucked safely in bark crevices and woody plant stems.

funFact: Treetop bush katydids are accomplished ventriloquists - their chirping calls seem to come from everywhere and nowhere at once because the sound bounces off leaves and branches, making it nearly impossible for predators (or curious humans) to pinpoint exactly which tree the singer is hiding in.
confusionNotes: Most people confuse katydids with grasshoppers, but remember: katydids are "antenna-heavy" with thread-thin feelers longer than their body, while grasshoppers have short, thick antennae. If you can't see where those antennae end, it's probably a katydid!
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, katydids don't actually say "Katy-did" - that's a myth based on people trying to put words to their rhythmic chirping sounds. Different species have completely different call patterns, and the treetop bush katydid's call sounds more like a soft ticking or clicking than any recognizable words.
compareHints: Among New England's bush katydids, the treetop bush katydid is distinguished by its prominent dark wing stripes and preference for high canopy living. The fork-tailed bush katydid has a distinctive split at the end of its abdomen, while the broad-winged bush katydid has much wider, more oval-shaped wings. Northern bush katydids tend to be found closer to ground level in shrubby areas rather than high in tree crowns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its bush katydid relatives in New England, the Fork-tailed is distinguished by that telltale forked rear appendage - Northern Bush Katydids have curved tails, while Broad-winged Bush Katydids have notably wider wings and straight tail projections.
Among the Scudderia bush katydids in New England, the northern species tends to be more common in cooler, northern areas compared to its relatives.
